module.objective: Introduce yourself by stating your name, country of origin, nationality, and age using the verb 'to be' accurately.

content.summary: Learn how to read simple introduction profiles in English. Focus on reading names, home countries, and favourite things — you don't need to understand every difficult word!

content.summary: In this module, you will learn how to build complete and accurate English sentences: from the basic Subject + Verb + Complement formula, to using capital letters correctly, and finally writing your own self-introduction profile independently.

mechanicsRules.title: Capital Letters Are Required
mechanicsRules.rule: Use a capital letter at the beginning of a sentence, for the pronoun 'I', for people's names (Liam), countries (Indonesia), and nationalities (Spanish).
mechanicsRules.example: I am from Jakarta and he is Japanese.

mechanicsRules.title: Full Stop at the End (.)
mechanicsRules.rule: Every statement must end with a full stop (.) right after the last word, with no space before it.

mechanicsRules.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
mechanicsRules.rule: Make sure the form of 'to be' matches the subject: I am, He/She/It is, We/They are.
mechanicsRules.example: They are students at London University.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Capitalise the beginning of each sentence ('She'), the nationality ('Italian'), and the country ('Italy').

content.summary: Practice voice articulation, pitch intonation (rising vs falling), and syllable rhythm before interacting live with AI Tutor Mr. Khoirul.
content.audioGuidance: Hello voice champion! Pronunciation is not just about words, it is about music and rhythm. Wh-questions glide downward, while confirmation questions lift upward. Let's build your vocal confidence step by step!

pillars.title: Pitch Trajectories
pillars.desc: Yes/No confirmation questions rise at the end (Rising ↗), while Wh-questions and statements fall steadily at the end (Falling ↘).
pillars.example: Are you Japanese? ↗ vs Where are you from? ↘

pillars.title: Syllable Stress Shift
pillars.desc: Stress shifts when a word changes from a country to a nationality, such as 'JA-pan' becoming 'ja-pa-NESE'.

pillars.title: Open & Relaxed Vowel Articulation
pillars.desc: Pronounce each vowel with a relaxed, open mouth position without holding your breath at the back of your throat.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress shifts from the 1st syllable (JA-) to the 3rd syllable (-NESE).
The stress shifts from the first syllable (AU-) to the middle syllable (-STRA-).
The vowel changes and the stress moves from (CA-) to the second syllable (-NA-).
The initial syllable stress (I-) moves to the second syllable (-TA-).
The stress stays on the syllable (-ZIL-), but the rhythm gets longer with the -ian ending.
The single-syllable word 'Spain' becomes 2 syllables with strong stress at the beginning: 'SPAN-ish'.

drills.hint: Stress your name clearly with a friendly intonation.
Raise your pitch at the end of the word 'Japan' ↗

drills.targetText: No, I am from Melbourne, Australia.
drills.focus: Stating Your City & Country of Origin
drills.hint: Use a steady falling intonation at the end of the sentence ↘
Wh-questions naturally glide down at the end of the word 'from' ↘
Say it with a smile and positive introduction energy!

practicumQuestions.instruction: Talk about yourself freely for 20–40 seconds. Choose one of the inspiration points below as a starting idea, then speak in your own words without following a rigid script.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Please tell me a little story about yourself. Who are you, where are you from, and what do you like?
inspirationPoints: Idea 1: Your full name, your city/country, and something interesting about where you live.
Idea 2: Your name, your current student status, and your favourite hobby or free-time activity.
Idea 3: Your name and a traditional food or drink from your area that you really like.
practicumQuestions.sampleStarter: Hello, my name is... I am from... and I...
practicumQuestions.hint: Use your own words! Tell your story casually, as if you are chatting with a new friend.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This trains your ability to speak in a narrative monologue independently without memorising a rigid script.

practicumQuestions.typeLabel: Free Storytelling: A Person You Admire
practicumQuestions.themeTitle: A Story About Someone You Admire
practicumQuestions.instruction: Talk about a best friend, family member, or international celebrity/athlete you admire freely for 20–40 seconds. Choose one of the inspiration points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now tell me a story about a person you admire: a good friend, a family member, or a famous athlete from another country.
inspirationPoints: Idea 1: An international friend — their name, their country, and their good qualities.
Idea 2: Your favourite world athlete — their name, sport, country, and achievements.
Idea 3: Your favourite celebrity/musician — their name, nationality, and work you enjoy.
practicumQuestions.sampleStarter: This is my friend / favourite athlete... He/She is from... and...
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the pronouns he/she and the verb 'is'. Share your story with enthusiasm!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This strengthens your command of third-person structures (he/she is) in free narrative storytelling.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Distinguish between a country name and a nationality in one spoken sentence. Listen to the audio example, then repeat it clearly!
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat: Spain is the country, and Spanish is the nationality.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Spain is the country, and Spanish is the nationality.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /speɪn ɪz ðə ˈkʌn.tri ænd ˈspæn.ɪʃ ɪz ðə ˌnæʃ.ənˈæl.ə.ti/
practicumQuestions.hint: Notice the -ish ending on the Spanish nationality word.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This strengthens the lexical difference between a geographical entity (country) and a citizen identity (nationality).

practicumQuestions.typeLabel: Linguistic Drill: Grammar (Verb To Be & Pronouns)
practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise your spoken reflex for using to be (am, is, are) with the correct subject pronoun. Say the following sentences one after another without hesitation!
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat: I am a student, she is from Italy, and we are friends.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I am a student, she is from Italy, and we are friends.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ æm ə ˈstjuː.dənt ʃiː ɪz frɒm ˈɪt.əl.i ænd wiː ɑːr frendz/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'am' for I, 'is' for she, and 'are' for we.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This locks in your automatic reflex for conjugating 'to be' so you don't mix them up when speaking spontaneously.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Listen and repeat the stress shift from CA-na-da (stress at the beginning) to ca-NA-di-an (stress in the middle)!
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat: CA-na-da is my country and I am ca-NA-di-an.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: CA-na-da is my country and I am ca-NA-di-an.
practicumQuestions.hint: Put a strong beat on the capitalised syllable: CA-na-da then ca-NA-di-an.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Stress shift is a key phonetic feature of English when a base word receives a nationality suffix.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise your pitch: use RISING intonation (↗) at the end of Yes/No questions and FALLING intonation (↘) at the end of statements!
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat: Are you Australian? Yes, I am Australian.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Are you Australian? ↗ Yes, I am Australian. ↘
practicumQuestions.hint: Raise your pitch high at the end of the question, then lower it when you answer yes.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Pitch intonation distinguishes the pragmatic meaning of a question versus a statement in spoken communication.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Talk about yourself freely for 20–40 seconds. Choose one of the inspiration points below as a starting idea, then speak in your own words without following a rigid script.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! Please tell me a little story about yourself. Who are you, where are you from, and what do you like?
inspirationPoints: Idea 1: Your full name, your city/country, and something interesting about where you live.
Idea 2: Your name, your current student status, and your favourite hobby or free-time activity.
Idea 3: Your name and a traditional food or drink from your area that you really like.
practicumQuestions.sampleStarter: Hello, my name is... I am from... and I...
practicumQuestions.hint: Use your own words! Tell your story casually, as if you are chatting with a new friend.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This trains your ability to speak in a narrative monologue independently without memorising a rigid script.
